subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Name the reagents used in the following reactions: i) oxidation of primary alcohol to carboxylic acid, ii) oxidation of primary alcohol to aldehyde.

verification.note: Unit 16 (Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.108-112, from the shaded sub-box "ALCOHOLS, PHENOLS AND ETHERS" of printed chapter 12 ("12. ORGANIC CHEMISTRY", a container of four unnumbered sub-boxes each restarting at 1). The book prints this question on book p.109 as Very Short Answer 2. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK ANSWER, EXPANDED: the printed answer is two words per part — "i) Acid KMnO₄" and "ii) PCC or CrO₃ in anhydrous medium". Three things are added. First, the equations, which the book gives for neither part. Second, the reason the aldehyde reagent must be anhydrous: in water the aldehyde is oxidised straight on to the acid, so the mild reagent only works in a dry medium and the aldehyde is distilled off as it forms. Third, the note that alkaline KMnO₄ gives the carboxylate SALT and needs dilute acid afterwards to give the free acid. BOOK SLOPPINESS: "CrO₃ in anhydrous medium" is written as though CrO₃ alone were a mild reagent; CrO₃ stops at the aldehyde only when the medium is anhydrous, and in aqueous acid the same reagent gives the carboxylic acid. TREND AND EXCEPTION: the card states the oxidation order (1° gives an aldehyde then an acid, 2° gives a ketone, 3° is not oxidised under these conditions) and names the exception on the same card — a tertiary alcohol DOES react with hot acidic oxidising mixtures, but it dehydrates first and the double bond is then broken, giving a mixture of smaller ketones and acids.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Reagent for the carboxylic acid
lines: Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ does the same work.
With alkaline KMnO₄ the product is the
carboxylate salt, so dilute acid is added
at the end to give the free acid.
steps.why: A carboxylic acid is two oxidation steps above a primary alcohol: the alcohol first gives the aldehyde, and the aldehyde is oxidised again. A strong oxidising agent in an aqueous acidic medium never stops at the aldehyde, so it goes all the way to the acid.
common_mistakes: Naming PCC here. PCC is the mild reagent and stops at the aldehyde.
Writing one [O] instead of two. Two oxygen atoms are needed, one for each step.
steps.memory_tip: Strong oxidant in water carries the oxidation through both steps: alcohol to aldehyde to acid.
steps.margin_note: The word acidified is part of the answer. KMnO₄ alone does not say which product you will get.

steps.label: Reagent for the aldehyde
lines: ii) PCC, that is pyridinium chlorochromate,
CrO₃ in an anhydrous medium also works.
The medium must be dry, because in water
the aldehyde is oxidised on to the acid.
steps.why: The aldehyde is the intermediate, so getting it out means stopping the reaction halfway. PCC is a mild reagent used in a dry solvent, and the aldehyde is distilled off as it forms. The oxidation order is: 1° gives an aldehyde and then an acid, 2° gives a ketone, 3° is not oxidised under these conditions. The exception is a hot acidic oxidising mixture, which does react with a tertiary alcohol — it removes water first and then breaks the double bond, giving a mixture of smaller ketones and acids.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the word anhydrous. In water the same chromium reagent gives the carboxylic acid, not the aldehyde.
Saying a tertiary alcohol can never be oxidised. Under hot acidic conditions it dehydrates and the double bond is then broken.
steps.memory_tip: PCC is the mild one and it is used dry, so the reaction stops one step early at the aldehyde.
steps.margin_note: Expand PCC to pyridinium chlorochromate once. The full name is worth writing where the question says name the reagent.

insider_note: One mark per part, so both reagents must be named. The commonest loss is naming K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄ for both parts: the second part is asking for the MILD reagent, and only PCC or anhydrous CrO₃ earns it.
